text:
🇸🇦 Most expats in Saudi Arabia: when your iqama renews, your employer pays SAR 9,150 or SAR 10,350 on top of your pay  🇸🇦 

Your family's fees come after that: SAR 4,800 a year for each dependant.

My assumption, so challenge it: by default those family fees are yours, not the company's. Many offers move them anyway.

If you are a UK or US founder opening in Riyadh next year, here is your first hire, priced.

The seat is an expat country manager at an illustrative data and cloud infrastructure company, on SAR 30,000 a month, basic plus housing. He has a spouse and two children. The entity is new, so expats outnumber Saudis.

What the law puts on the company, a year:
Levy and work permit: SAR 9,700
Iqama: SAR 650
GOSI at 2%: SAR 7,200
End of service: SAR 15,000
Medical for four, illustrative: SAR 18,400
Total above pay: SAR 50,950

That is 14% on top of SAR 360,000 of pay.

What stays with him by default:
Dependant fees for three: SAR 14,400

Put that line in the offer and the seat costs SAR 65,350 above pay, which is 18%.

So the family shows up twice. The Council of Health Insurance requires the employer to insure them. Article 40 of the Labour Law, which lists the fees the employer bears, does not list theirs.

Settle both lines before the offer letter, not after the move.

If you saved my 10 November post on the expat seat: that seat had no family. This one does.

If you sign off a Riyadh headcount plan for 2027, whose line are the family fees on?

#Saudization #Riyadh #CF

text:
Hussain Sajwani said last week that what he made in thirty years, he made in Anthropic in less than two. On Thursday Anthropic began trading on Nasdaq at $83 a share, valued at about $1.5 trillion fully diluted. The shares closed at $97.17, up 17 percent, valuing the company at about $1.8 trillion fully diluted.

Global SWF counts $8.15 billion of Gulf money committed to Anthropic since 2024. The Qatar Investment Authority put in $3 billion, and IHC added $600 million through Alpha Wave Global. DAMAC Group's Manius Invest bought $50 million of shares out of the FTX bankruptcy estate in 2024, and Abu Dhabi vehicles account for most of the rest.

The holdings are undisclosed, so any return figure is guesswork, and Sajwani's line is the only scorecard on tape.

For a US private-markets reader, the lesson is in how the money got in. A Dubai property family and Qatar's sovereign fund ended up on the same cap table, and both bought directly, through a court-supervised secondary and then in primary rounds. Expect the same names to bid for the next contested asset themselves, alongside the funds they back as limited partners.

The Gulf's savings in Washington are being spent to keep cash moving in Riyadh, and the figures landed in the week a missile broke the windows of the sovereign fund's tower.

I've seen this play out more than once.

A founder decides to enter Saudi Arabia. A well-meaning contact says, "you'll need a local partner." The founder starts looking for one. Six months pass. Equity discussions stall. The market opportunity moves on.

Then they discover: they never needed a partner at all.

Saudi Arabia allows full foreign ownership across most activities via a MISA licence. No sponsor. No equity concession. Just a licence, a capital requirement, and attested documents.

The real risks are the ones founders overlook before they file: — Is your activity on the negative list? — Does your business type clear the capital threshold? (Services: SAR 100k–500k. Retail full-ownership: SAR 30M.) — Are your corporate documents properly attested?

A clean file moves fast. A messy one drags for months.

Don't let a myth cost you six months.

Have any of you heard about Saudi Arabia providing private equity funds (75 percent of $500Mn) to Pakistan for equity investment.

As we know when someone do private equity investment somewhere they wants to have ownership rights there and also they want a successful exit in the end. Is Pakistan ready for such things? To make this thing successful Pakistan needs to have a system of transparent financial reporting system as investors do want reliable financial statements to assess the financial position of any organization. Pakistan also need to make sure that we have willing private business owners who wants who wants outside investors to have ownership rights in their business. From equity-free residencies to AED 250K SAFE cheques, Gulf accelerators offer founders very different deals. Here's how the main programmes compare 🚀

Founders often ask me which Gulf accelerator to apply to. Every GCC capital now has programmes competing for them, but the terms vary a lot. Some write cheques for equity, some pay for your residency and take nothing, and some are really a door into government procurement.

What stands out to me:
→ Abu Dhabi's package is the biggest once in-kind support is counted, and it takes equity for it. Hub71 offers AED 250K in cash through an uncapped SAFE, plus AED 250K of in-kind support, and you need a real presence in Abu Dhabi
→ Much of the region is equity-free. Dubai Future Accelerators, Sharjah Entrepreneurship Center (Sheraa) in Sharjah, Misk Foundation and KAUST's Taqadam take 0%. Taqadam gives a $40K non-dilutive grant, with up to $100K more for the top teams
→ Saudi Arabia has the deepest bench. Flat6Labs Riyadh wrote SAR 500K seed cheques, with up to SAR 2.4M in follow-on funding, until its final cohort in January 2026. The Garage, MonshaatSA and university programmes are still running
→ Qatar and Oman mostly invest through funds. I am pleased to share our latest research publication in the International Journal of Financial Studies (MDPI).

Title:
“The Accounting Role of Financial and Non-Financial Information as Perceived by Venture Capitalists: Evidence from Saudi Arabia”

This study examines how venture capitalists rely on financial and non-financial information when evaluating start-ups, drawing on survey evidence from 405 angel investors and investment fund professionals in Saudi Arabia.

Our findings highlight the importance of both traditional financial information and non-financial factors, including governance, sector specialization, target markets, and the characteristics of start-ups, in investment evaluation.

This research contributes to the growing literature on accounting information, venture capital, and entrepreneurship, while offering practical insights for investors and start-ups in the Saudi entrepreneurial ecosystem.

I am grateful to my co-authors, Dr. Amal A. Alamoudi and Dr. Badr B. Banhmeid, for their valuable collaboration and contributions to this research.

text:
Anthropic priced its public offering at $83 per share, crossing a $1.5 trillion valuation after seeing demand oversubscribed by 10 times. That single valuation equals roughly 37% of India's projected FY27 GDP. Uday Kotak pointed out that it exceeds the combined market capitalization of India's top 10 listed firms, setting off a sharp debate about why our ecosystem lacks domestic foundational model builders.

The anxiety is understandable, but trying to match Western frontier labs in a raw compute arms race misses where our real advantage lies. Building foundation models demands billions in specialized infrastructure and heavy capital subsidies. India's structural edge has always been distribution, workflow execution, and hyper-efficient unit economics.

Winning the application layer requires owning the messy, complex operational software that enterprises actually pay for. We can let foreign balance sheets fund base-layer research while Indian founders capture the value built on top of it.

Should Indian founders stop chasing sovereign foundation models and concentrate capital purely on the application layer?

Orange is adding €250 million to Orange Ventures, its venture capital arm, and the money will be deployed between 2027 and 2032.

Africa’s share is smaller than the headline suggests. €200 million is set aside for European startups, while €50 million goes to Africa and the Middle East combined, and Orange hasn’t said how that €50 million will be split between the two regions.

The fund will back startups in AI, cybersecurity, cloud computing, fintech and digital health.

More than half of Orange Ventures’ 40 portfolio companies already have commercial partnerships with the group, and Orange runs telecom operations in many African markets. A startup that can plug into that network gets distribution as well as a cheque.

text:
The Antariksh Venture Capital Fund, anchored by IN-SPACe and managed by SIDBI Venture Capital Limited, announced a ₹60 Crore investment to lead the first close of Bengaluru-headquartered Earth-intelligence company SatSure’s ₹200 Crore Series B funding round. The commitment marks AVCF’s first capital deployment into the downstream data analytics and artificial intelligence layer of India’s space economy.

Founded by Prateep Basu and Rashmit Singh Sukhmani, SatSure operates a full-stack Earth intelligence model through its subsidiary KaleidEO, which builds optical satellite payloads and full satellites for India’s national Earth Observation constellation under the EO-PPP, while SatSure turns Earth observation data into decision intelligence for banks, insurers, critical infrastructure companies, and governments. SIDBI Venture Capital Limited Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer Arup Kumar said the fund is backing full-stack enterprises that pair indigenous orbital infrastructure with downstream decision intelligence.

The Series B capital will accelerate four strategic deliverables: advancing SatSure’s optical payloads ahead of orbital flight in 2027, executing the multi-satellite constellation mandate under the IN-SPACe-anchored Earth Observation Public-Private Partnership, scaling Dhaarini, and expanding international commercial operations from India. Prateep Basu said the round lets the company build its full stack further from India for the world.

headline: 2,334 followers
text:
African venture capital raised more money this year, but backed fewer companies.

AVCA counts $2.6 billion invested in the first nine months of 2026, across only 271 deals. That is the lowest deal count since 2020. Large rounds for mature companies lifted the total. Seed-stage founders were left with less.

That is the segment Mediterrania Capital Partners has chosen to enter. The private equity firm, known for backing mid-sized African companies, has launched MC Outlierz Ventures with Morocco's Outlierz Ventures. The focus is Seed and Pre-Series A, in B2B fintech, digital health and AI that automates business processes.

The interesting part is not the cheque. Startups get access to MCP's portfolio companies in Africa and the Gulf, which can become their first customers.

For an early-stage startup, a large first client can matter as much as the cheque.

Fund size and first investments are not public yet.

author: Andrew Nichol
headline: Private Equity and Corporate Finance
text:
Thank you to everyone who joined us at the Royal Automobile Club in London this week for Lumina Capital Advisers' M&A breakfast, where we discussed the impact of regional instability and global geopolitics on Middle East M&A activity. Great conversations and discussions as ever;

 🔹 Deals slowed, not stopped; 66% saw transactions paused or delayed this year but only 20% had a deal abandoned
 🔹 Region remains in focus; 69% plan to maintain or grow their regional footprint, only 4% are considering an exit. The UAE (72%) was the top target market this year
 🔹 Cross-border deals flex SWF deal-making capabilities into consolidation sectors;  Mubadala and Centerbridge just-announced acquisition of Canaccord Genuity’s UK wealth management business 
 🔹 True cross-border flows into and out of region; Apollo’s minority stake acquisition into Mubadala Capital, formalising a 10-year plus global relationship
 🔹 Regional risk is being priced in; 77% adjusted price or structure, through higher discount rates, longer earn-outs and stronger deal protections
 🔹 Critical sectors see momentum; Energy and infrastructure (including data centers) was the most active sector (31%, up from 16%), and healthcare, logistics, food/resource security and technology show the strongest intent for the next 12 months

author: Emilio S. Rivera
headline: M&A Strategist for Digital Founders | Venture Building | Growth Systems & Market Development
text:
Over the past few months, my professional life has changed dramatically.

Not long ago, M&A was something I literally had no idea about.

Today, I spend my days speaking with buyers, founders and investors, working across international markets, building acquisition outreach strategies, learning how deals are structured, and getting a front-row seat to how entrepreneurs build, acquire and eventually exit companies.

And I’ve realized that I want to start documenting more of that journey.
Not as someone pretending to have all the answers.

Actually, the opposite...

I want to share what I’m learning while I’m learning it.

I wanted a real-life MBA experience without having to pay a fortune.
Well... here you go.

M&A. Entrepreneurship. International business. AI. Professional travel. Building systems. The mistakes, the intense days, the interesting conversations, and the personal side of trying to build an ambitious life while still making time for the people and things that matter.

Some of it will be technical.
Some of it will be personal.
And some of it will probably just be me working from somewhere unexpected with a laptop.

But I think there’s value in documenting the process, not only the destination.
So that’s what I’m going to start doing.
And here’s a pic from one of those unexpected offices — Copacabana, Rio de Janeiro. 🇧🇷

Not a bad front-row seat.
